notes.meaning: King Solomon is named as the author of these wise sayings. As the king of Israel and the son of King David, God gave him great understanding to guide people in daily life. These proverbs give practical rules for living well under God's rule.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that Proverbs shares patterns and themes with ancient Near Eastern wisdom texts, showing that Israelite writers used well-known cultural styles to teach faith in the one true God.

notes.meaning: The opening words explain the purpose of the book: to help people gain true wisdom and self-control. Wisdom means more than gathering facts; it is the skill of making good, godly choices in everyday life. Discipline means training the heart and mind to stay on the right path.

These sayings teach people how to live sensibly, honestly, and fairly. Righteousness means doing what is right in God's eyes, while justice and equity mean treating all people with truth and fairness. Learning God's wisdom shapes how we treat our neighbors every day.

Solomon addresses people who are young, inexperienced, or easily led astray. The simple are not necessarily foolish, but they are open to every influence because they lack experience. This teaching gives them healthy caution and careful thought so they can avoid dangerous traps.

These proverbs are not just for beginners, but also for people who are already wise. A truly wise person is humble enough to keep listening and learning throughout life. By paying attention, experienced people gain skill in guiding themselves and helping others.

The reader learns how to think through parables, wise sayings, and puzzling questions. Many important truths in life require quiet reflection rather than quick answers. Working through these wise sayings trains the mind to understand God's truth more clearly.

Deep reverence and respect for the Lord are the true starting point of all real learning. The fear of the Lord does not mean terror, but a loving awe that honors God as Creator and gladly obeys Him. Those who reject God's guidance stay foolish because they throw away the very foundation of truth.

differ.view: Reformed teachers stress that this fear is filial fear, like a loving child who honors a father, and that true wisdom can never be separated from holiness and growing in the knowledge of God.
Anglican writers note that while holy fear is the foundation under the law, the gospel leads believers forward into perfect love, which fulfills and crowns that starting point.

notes.meaning: Solomon urges children to listen closely to the training given by both their father and mother. Honoring parents is the very first family duty after honoring God Himself. A godly home provides the earliest and most vital lessons in walking with the Lord.

Obeying godly parental advice brings grace and honor to a young person's life, like a handsome garland or a fine necklace. True beauty and dignity do not come from costly clothes, but from the good character formed by wise teaching. Following God's ways makes a person's life honorable and respected by others.

A strong warning is given against yielding to bad companions who try to lead a young person into sin. Sinners often try hard to persuade others to join their destructive schemes. A person cannot be forced into wrongdoing; sin only happens when someone gives consent to the temptation.

The wicked invite newcomers into violent gangs, plotting to ambush travelers for dishonest gain. They attack people who have done them no wrong simply out of greed and cruelty. Solomon strips away all exciting excuses and shows robbery for the brutal crime it really is.

The bandits boast that they will wipe out their victims completely, like the grave swallowing up the dead. In the Old Testament, Sheol is the place of the dead. These violent men imagine they can destroy their targets without leaving any trace of their crime behind.

The tempters promise quick wealth and houses filled with stolen treasures. They appeal to the desire for easy riches, pretending that theft is a fast path to prosperity. In chasing stolen goods, however, they overlook the great danger they bring upon their own lives.

The gang promises equal sharing and strong brotherhood, asking the recruit to share one common purse. Criminal groups often lure lonely young people through the promise of friendship, belonging, and shared profit. This false sense of community only binds people together in guilt and danger.

The father urgently warns his child not even to take the first step alongside such companions. Walking with them leads to ruin, so the safest choice is to stay far away from their company. Temptation must be resisted right at the beginning before evil habits take hold.

These criminals are eager to commit evil and rush quickly to shed innocent blood. Their desires drive them forward headlong into violence without any thought of mercy. Joining them means sharing in the guilt of terrible crimes that bring swift judgment.

Even a simple bird knows enough to stay away if a hunter sets a net in plain sight. Sinners, however, act more foolishly than birds because they run straight into traps that are clearly visible. They blind themselves to the obvious danger of their wicked choices.

In their blind pursuit of violence, these criminals end up plotting their own destruction. While they think they are hunting innocent people, divine justice turns their schemes back upon their own heads. The trap they set for others becomes the very instrument of their own ruin.

This is the certain end for everyone who hungers for dishonest wealth. Greed takes over a person's heart and eventually destroys the one who holds onto it. Robbery and ill-gotten gains cost far more than they could ever provide.

Wisdom is pictured here as a noble woman speaking openly in the busy streets and public squares. God's truth is not hidden away in secret corners or kept only for a privileged few. It is offered freely and clearly to ordinary people in the middle of everyday life.

Wisdom raises her voice in the busiest places, especially at the city gates where court was held and crowds gathered. She cries aloud because she cares deeply about people and wants to rescue them from destruction. No one can claim that God never warned them or offered them direction.

Wisdom directly challenges three kinds of people: the careless who enjoy staying ignorant, the proud mockers who make fun of sacred things, and stubborn fools who hate learning. Each group stubbornly refuses the truth for different reasons. She asks how long they will continue ruining themselves with such foolish attitudes.

Wisdom pleads with the stubborn to turn around and accept her gentle correction. If they listen and repent, she promises to pour out her insights and make her words plain to their minds. Turning to God's wisdom opens the door to deeper understanding and spiritual guidance.

differ.view: Anglican commentators connect the pouring out of wisdom's spirit directly with the prophecy in Joel and its fulfillment in the Holy Spirit at Pentecost.
Some evangelical writers view this phrase as referring to the spirit and mind of wisdom being shared, rather than a direct reference to the Holy Spirit.

notes.meaning: Wisdom's tone changes from an invitation of mercy to an announcement of judgment. She called out repeatedly and held out her hand to help, but people turned away and ignored her. When God reaches out in kindness, refusing to respond brings heavy consequences.

The rebellious completely disregarded Wisdom's advice and refused every word of correction. Their rejection was not an accident or a simple misunderstanding, but a deliberate choice. Persisting in stubborn disobedience leaves a person without any defense when trouble arrives.

Wisdom warns that when disaster strikes, she will laugh at their terror and offer no relief. This does not mean God enjoys human misery, but that divine justice will prevail while mocked truth offers no comfort to those who hated it. When the crisis comes, rejected wisdom can no longer rescue the stubborn fool.

Sudden ruin is described as coming like a ferocious storm or a violent whirlwind. When overwhelming distress and anguish crash into their lives, the fools will have no shelter to protect them. Ignoring wisdom leaves a person totally unprepared for the storms of life.

In their sudden panic, the wicked will cry out for wisdom, but no answer will come. They will search desperately for help, but it will be too late because they refused it when it was freely offered. Crying out merely to escape pain is not the same as truly seeking God with a humble heart.

The root cause of their ruin is that they hated true knowledge and chose not to fear the Lord. Their downfall did not happen by bad luck; it was the direct outcome of their own stubborn choices. Rejecting God's authority always cuts a person off from real life and safety.

These people continually turned down good counsel and treated every godly rebuke with contempt. They wanted to run their own lives without any moral boundaries or divine correction. Such open disrespect for God's truth seals a person's spiritual ruin.

God allows the wicked to reap the natural harvest of what they have sown. They will eat the bitter fruit of their own evil choices until they are sick of their own schemes. Sin carries its own terrible punishment within itself.

Turning away from God proves fatal for the simple, while false security and complacency ruin the stubborn fool. When people feel completely comfortable in their sin, they deceive themselves into thinking nothing bad will happen. That self-satisfied carelessness leads straight to destruction.

The chapter closes with a comforting promise of peace for everyone who listens to Wisdom and obeys her. Such people will live in safety and rest quietly without being terrified by evil tidings. True peace of mind comes from trusting God and walking in His wise ways.
